name: @stonedogcode/auth
description: Authentication factor primitives: password, PIN, TOTP, WebAuthn challenges and single-use emailed tokens. No storage, no transport, no framework.
author: StoneDogCode L.L.C.
//exports: TypeScript SOURCE rather than a bundled dist/, matching @stonedogcode/howto and stonedog-style. The argon2 adapters are separate entry points so a consumer that never builds a password factor never resolves a binding it has not installed.
//files: The __tests__ exclusion is load-bearing rather than tidiness: anything shipped under src/ is compiled by the CONSUMER, and the tests import jest globals. They would also ship a suite nobody can run to every consumer.

scripts.gate: npm run type-check && npm run lint && npm run test && npm run build

//publish:stonedog-auth: Run from a terminal, interactively — npm prompts for the 2FA one-time password and the login flow needs a browser. It refuses a checkout that is detached, dirty, or behind origin/main; refuses a version already published; refuses a tarball missing an entry point, the NOTICE, or containing tests; refuses any runtime dependency at all, and refuses either argon2 binding being anything but an optional peer. Then it proves the result by installing from the registry into a temp directory and checking that installing alone pulls in NO argon2 binding.
//dependencies: There are none, and that is a deliberate property rather than a coincidence. Everything here is node:crypto or arithmetic. A package that sits on the sign-in path of four products should be auditable in an afternoon, and every dependency it takes is one every consumer inherits on that path.
//peerDependencies: Both argon2 bindings are optional. Which one works is decided by the runtime image — a node-gyp build needs a toolchain an Alpine image does not carry — and the two are interoperable because both emit the standard PHC string. A consumer installs whichever suits its image, or neither.
//publishConfig: A scoped package defaults to RESTRICTED on npm, which needs a paid plan and would fail the publish. Declaring it here means the intent travels with the manifest rather than depending on someone remembering --access public.
